reason: The provided sources contain over 10 cross-verified claims across independent sites detailing the construction, scale, speed, and daily experience aboard the International Space Station.
story: Assembled in low Earth orbit starting with the launch of the Zarya module in 1998, the International Space Station is the largest human-made spacecraft ever built. Spanning the length and width of an American football field with an internal volume comparable to a Boeing 747 airliner, this massive international laboratory orbits Earth at roughly 17,500 miles per hour at an altitude of 250 miles. Because it completes a full orbit around the planet approximately every 90 minutes along a 51.6-degree orbital path, crew members aboard experience 15 to 16 sunrises and sunsets every 24 hours. Continuously inhabited since November 2000 through a partnership between NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA, the ISS serves as a primary hub for zero-gravity research. However, due to structural aging and air leaks, space agencies plan to deorbit the station around 2030, guiding its destruction in Earth's atmosphere.
angle: Orbiting Earth at 17,500 miles per hour, astronauts aboard the International Space Station experience 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours.

claims.claim: The first component of the International Space Station, the Russian-built Zarya module, was launched in November 1998.
The ISS has been continuously inhabited by human crews since November 2, 2000.
The ISS is operated through an international partnership between five space agencies: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA.
The ISS orbits Earth at an altitude of approximately 250 miles (400 kilometers).
The space station travels at an orbital speed of approximately 17,200 to 17,500 miles per hour (27,600 to 28,000 km/h).
The ISS completes an orbit around Earth roughly every 92 to 93 minutes.
Because of its rapid 90-minute orbit, astronauts aboard the ISS experience 15 or 16 sunrises and sunsets every 24 hours.
The station flies in an orbit inclined at 51.6 degrees latitude north and south.
The overall footprint of the ISS spans the length and width of a full-sized American football field.
The pressurized internal volume of the ISS is comparable to a Boeing 747 jumbo jetliner.
Two weeks after Zarya launched, the U.S.-built Unity node was ferried up and joined to it in orbit.
Europe's Columbus research laboratory module was contributed to the ISS by the European Space Agency.
In January 2020, NASA awarded Axiom Space a contract to attach commercial modules to the ISS.
Plans are underway to retire and deorbit the ISS around the year 2030.

disputed: Total mass of the station varies slightly across sources (S5 lists 430 metric tons, S6 lists 925,000 pounds / 420,000 kg, and S1 quotes 500 tons); the script should state 'over 400 metric tons' or avoid precise mass figures.
Orbital period is stated as 93 minutes in S1 and 92 minutes in S6; the script should attribute or round to 'roughly 90 minutes'.
